----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the API documentation for the pymizu library.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Channels

A two-way message link between a Python process and a helper process that it spawns.


Channel()

A shared-memory channel handle (process-private).

Create the host side with [`Channel.create()`](`pymizu.Channel.create`),
which spawns the peer. The peer side attaches with ``Channel._attach()``,
as ``python -m pymizu.child`` does. Handles do not survive ``fork()``.

Threading: a side belongs to one thread at a time. Call its verbs
([`send()`](`pymizu.Channel.send`), [`recv()`](`pymizu.Channel.recv`),
their batch forms) from one thread only; a second verb from another thread
raises [`ConcurrentUseError`](`pymizu.ConcurrentUseError`). Blocking and
async receives are likewise exclusive on a side: a blocking receive while a
[`recv_async()`](`pymizu.Channel.recv_async`) consumer is active raises it
too, from any thread but the consumer's event loop, whose own receives can
never race it. Two-way traffic from two threads needs two channels.
Teardown is the exception: [`destroy()`](`pymizu.Channel.destroy`) is safe
from any thread.


## Task pools

A set of worker processes that divide submitted tasks among themselves.


Pool()

A shared-memory work-stealing task pool handle (process-private).

Create the controller side with [`Pool.create()`](`pymizu.Pool.create`),
which spawns the workers (``python -m pymizu.worker``). Other processes
join as submitters with [`Pool.attach()`](`pymizu.Pool.attach`). The pool
exists only as long as the process that created it: dropping the handle
shuts the pool down as [`Pool.stop()`](`pymizu.Pool.stop`) does, but
without waiting for the workers. Handles do not survive ``fork()``.

Task callables travel by pickle. With the standard pickle a submitted
callable must be an importable reference (as with `multiprocessing`), and
installing cloudpickle lifts that restriction.

Threading: a handle has two single-threaded halves. The producing half
([`submit()`](`pymizu.Pool.submit`),
[`submit_batch()`](`pymizu.Pool.submit_batch`),
[`map()`](`pymizu.Pool.map`)) belongs to one thread, and a concurrent
second producer raises [`ConcurrentUseError`](`pymizu.ConcurrentUseError`).
The waiting half (the blocking collects and [`stop()`](`pymizu.Pool.stop`))
likewise belongs to one thread, which may be a different one from the
producer's. To produce from several threads,
[`attach()`](`pymizu.Pool.attach`) one handle per thread (each is its own
producer, with its own submission queue), or use
[`PoolExecutor`](`pymizu.PoolExecutor`), whose submits are thread-safe.
Teardown is the exception: [`destroy()`](`pymizu.Pool.destroy`) is safe
from any thread.

_Task()

A task handle from Pool.submit(). It is collected exactly once, and an uncollected handle releases its slot when garbage collected.

Map(pool: 'pymizu.Pool', plan: '_Plan') -> 'None'

The handle for one submitted map run.

Returned by [`Pool.map()`](`pymizu.Pool.map`) and
[`PreparedMap.run()`](`pymizu.PreparedMap.run`). Each handle collects
exactly once. `collect()` blocks for the results. `collect_async()` and
`await` provide the same results without blocking. A streaming map requires
`collect()` because its sliding task window advances in the blocking loop.

`cancel()` stops the run. Workers halt within about one batch, and the
outstanding tasks are cancelled. An uncollected handle cancels its run at
garbage collection.

PreparedMap(pool: 'pymizu.Pool', fn: '_Callable[..., _Any]', x: '_Any', *, args: '_Any' = (), kwargs: 'dict | None' = None, n_chunks: 'int | None' = None, template: '_Any' = None, stream: 'bool' = False) -> 'None'

A reusable map staged in shared memory.

Create with [`Pool.map_prepare()`](`pymizu.Pool.map_prepare`). `run()`
returns a [`Map`](`pymizu.Map`) handle for one run. Preparation stores the
map description and shared data. Later runs reuse the staged data and the
workers' cached setup when possible. Close with `close()` or a `with`
block to release the shared memory.

Parameters
----------
pool
    The [`Pool`](`pymizu.Pool`) to run on.
fn
    The function to map, or a [`call`](`pymizu.call`) spec, as for
    [`Pool.map()`](`pymizu.Pool.map`).
x
    The data to map over.
args
    Constant positional arguments appended to every call.
kwargs
    Constant keyword arguments for every call.
n_chunks
    Overrides the number of batches the elements are split into.
template
    An example buffer declaring each result's dtype and length, as for
    [`Pool.map()`](`pymizu.Pool.map`).
stream
    Stream slices of `x` instead of writing it to shared memory whole, as
    for [`Pool.map()`](`pymizu.Pool.map`).

Examples
--------
Run a prepared map again with replacement data:

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pymizu

with pymizu.Pool.create(2) as pool:
    with pool.map_prepare(np.square, np.arange(4.0)) as pm:
        first = pm.run().collect(timeout=10)
        second = pm.run(np.array([4.0, -5.0, 6.0, 7.0])).collect(
            timeout=10
        )
second
```

PoolExecutor(pool: 'pymizu.Pool', *, stop_pool: 'bool' = False) -> 'None'

A `concurrent.futures.Executor` backed by a pymizu pool.

`submit()` returns a standard `concurrent.futures.Future`. The stdlib
`wait`, `as_completed`, and `asyncio.wrap_future` helpers accept it.
`map()` supports `ProcessPoolExecutor`-style chunking. `create()` spawns
an owned pool.

Parameters
----------
pool
    The pool to wrap. Its lifetime stays with its owner unless `stop_pool`
    is set, in which case `shutdown()` stops it.
stop_pool
    When True, `shutdown()` stops the wrapped pool.

Notes
-----
`submit()` and the stdlib `map()` are thread-safe. An internal lock
serializes the single-producer pool handle. Use this adapter when several
threads submit to one pool.

Task failures raise `pymizu.TaskError`. `Future.running()` always returns
False because futures resolve at completion. Cancellation follows
[`Task.cancel()`](`pymizu.Task`) and never interrupts a running task.
`shutdown(cancel_futures=True)` cancels every outstanding future because
the pool cannot distinguish queued from running tasks. A running task
completes, but its result is discarded.

An internal error, such as another caller stopping the wrapped pool, fails
every outstanding future. Later submissions raise instead of queueing
work.

Futures resolve, and `add_done_callback` callbacks run, on pymizu's
listener thread. Keep callbacks short. Never block a callback on the pool
itself. If the result table is full, `submit()` waits for the executor to
collect a result. A submission from a listener-thread done callback raises
`SlotsExhaustedError` because waiting there would deadlock the drain.

`map()` honors `chunksize` and `buffersize` like `ProcessPoolExecutor`.
For bulk maps, [`Pool.map`](`pymizu.Pool.map`) is faster.

Examples
--------
Use as a `concurrent.futures.Executor`:

```{python}
import pymizu

with pymizu.PoolExecutor.create(2) as ex:
    futures = [ex.submit(pow, 2, i) for i in range(4)]
    results = [f.result() for f in futures]
results
```


## Cross-language interop

R peers and workers (the mizu R package), neutral task specifications, and the data.frame's Python home.


call(name: 'str | None' = None, /, *args: '_Any', source: 'str | None' = None, **kwargs: '_Any')

A task specification for a pool of another language's workers.

Describes a call for [`Pool.submit()`](`pymizu.Pool.submit`): a qualified
name (``"mod.fn"`` for Python workers, ``"pkg::fn"`` for R workers) or a
``source=`` string in the workers' language, plus the constant arguments.
The spec describes a call, not a value. The language is not named at the
call site, because `Pool.submit` reads the workers' language from the pool
itself, and a bare unqualified name errors at submit, not here.

Parameters
----------
name
    A qualified name: ``"mod.fn"`` for Python workers,
    ``"pkg::fn"`` for R workers.
args
    Constant positional arguments of the call.
source
    A source string in the workers' language. Exactly one of
    ``name`` or ``source`` must be given.
kwargs
    Constant keyword arguments of the call.

Details
-------
Unnamed arguments map to the positional list and keyword arguments to the
named dict, matching R's calling convention. Arguments must be portable
values (the portable subset documented under
[`Channel.send()`](`pymizu.Channel.send`)). A non-portable argument raises
[`DeclinedError`](`pymizu.DeclinedError`) at submit.

A ``source=`` task evaluates in a fresh namespace with the keyword
arguments bound as names and positional arguments bound as ``_1``,
``_2``, ... The result is the trailing expression's value, or None
when the source ends with a statement.

Large arguments cross to foreign workers by reference rather than by copy.
A fresh buffer argument past the zero-copy floor is written to shared
memory once, and the worker reads a view over it. An argument that is
already a shared view crosses as its name alone, so no bytes move. On a
pool whose workers predate this mechanism, such a task fails at submit with
an error naming the remedy.

Examples
--------
A spec task also runs on a normal (Python-worker) pool:

>>> import pymizu
>>> with pymizu.Pool.create(2) as pool:
...     task = pool.submit(pymizu.call("math.sqrt", 2.0))
...     results = pool.collect_all([task], timeout=10)
>>> results
[1.4142135623730951]

launcher(*, python: 'str | None' = None, stdout: '_Any' = None, stderr: '_Any' = None) -> '_Callable[..., _subprocess.Popen]'

Return a launcher spawning Python processes running pymizu.

[`Channel.create()`](`pymizu.Channel.create`) calls it with `token` alone
to spawn the peer; [`Pool.create()`](`pymizu.Pool.create`) calls it with
`token` and `slot` to spawn each worker. The process runs ``python -m
pymizu.child <token>`` or ``python -m pymizu.worker <token> <slot>``. This
is the default of every ``launcher=`` argument, and the counterpart of the
R package's ``mizu_launcher()``.

Parameters
----------
python
    Path to the Python interpreter; the default is
    `sys.executable`.
stdout
    Forwarded to `subprocess.Popen`; the default inherits the
    console, where the peer's error messages land.
stderr
    Forwarded to `subprocess.Popen`.

Returns
-------
    A `callable(token, slot=None)` launcher for
    [`Channel.create()`](`pymizu.Channel.create`) and
    [`Pool.create()`](`pymizu.Pool.create`).

Examples
--------
```python
import pymizu

with pymizu.Pool.create(
    4, launcher=pymizu.launcher(stderr="worker.log")
) as pool:
    print(pool.submit(abs, -1).collect())
```

r_launcher(*, rscript: 'str | None' = None, stdout: '_Any' = None, stderr: '_Any' = None) -> '_Callable[..., _subprocess.Popen]'

Return a launcher spawning R processes running the `mizu` package.

[`Channel.create()`](`pymizu.Channel.create`) calls it with `token`
alone to spawn the peer; [`Pool.create()`](`pymizu.Pool.create`)
calls it with `token` and `slot` to spawn each worker. The process
runs `rscript` on the package's static child runner with the entry
expression (`mizu:::peer_main(<token>)` or
`mizu:::worker_main(<token>, <slot>)`) and the detected library
paths passed along in argv (without them it cannot `library(mizu)` from the
host's libraries). It is the counterpart of the R package's
`mizu_py_launcher()`.

Parameters
----------
rscript
    Path to Rscript; the default searches the PATH.
stdout
    Forwarded to `subprocess.Popen`; the default inherits the
    console, where the peer's error messages land.
stderr
    Forwarded to `subprocess.Popen`.

Returns
-------
    A `callable(token, slot=None)` launcher for
    [`Channel.create()`](`pymizu.Channel.create`) and
    [`Pool.create()`](`pymizu.Pool.create`).

Raises
------
MizuError
    Raised here, before any channel or pool is created, when Rscript is not
    found or no installed `mizu` with source string support is available.

Notes
-----
The first worker to join records the workers' language in the pool, so the
launcher carries no language attribute. A pool of R workers takes
[`pymizu.call()`](`pymizu.call`) specifications through
[`Pool.submit()`](`pymizu.Pool.submit`), and a plain callable raises an
error naming `call`. A launcher that spawns the wrong language fails at
join, not at the first task.

Examples
--------
```python
import pymizu

with pymizu.Pool.create(4, launcher=pymizu.r_launcher()) as pool:
    spec = pymizu.call(source="summary(cars$speed)")
    print(pool.submit(spec).collect())
```

Frame()

A data.frame's Python home: named columns with a row count.

to_dict() returns the columns as a dict without an Arrow
library, and __arrow_c_stream__ exports to polars, pyarrow, or
pandas. from_arrow() constructs one from an Arrow producer, the
opt-in zero-copy path for Python-to-Python channels. R frame
metadata (classes, extra attributes) survives an unmodified
round trip, while a rebuilt frame arrives in R as a plain
data.frame.

DimArray(shape, dtype=None, buffer=None, offset=0, strides=None, order=None)

An `ndarray` carrying R labels.

A received labeled vector or array arrives as a DimArray. An unmodified
echo restores every label in R (`identical()`). The labels are `names`,
`dimnames`, `axis_names`, and `r_class`.

To send a labeled value, set `names` on a 1-D array. Set `dimnames` on a
matrix or n-D array, with optional `axis_names` for R's
`names(dimnames(x))`. For R's table class, set `r_class = "table"`. Use
either `names` or `dimnames`, not both. `axis_names` requires `dimnames`
and has one entry per axis.

Numpy operations that build a new array drop all labels. This includes
transposes, arithmetic, slices, and copies. A new array never inherits
labels that no longer match its data.


## Outcomes and errors

A full ring, a timeout, a close, or a dead peer returns as a sentinel singleton — FULL / TIMEOUT / CLOSED / PEER_GONE — tested by identity, never raised. Real failures raise exceptions.


Sentinel()

A terminal-state sentinel returned by pymizu verbs. Test by identity against pymizu.FULL / TIMEOUT / CLOSED / PEER_GONE.

is_sentinel(object, /)

is_sentinel(x) -> bool

True only for the exact sentinel singletons this process's verbs
return, so a look-alike payload never passes. The test is identity, not
class.

is_remote_error(x: '_Any') -> 'bool'

Test whether a received channel value is a remote error.

An uncaught error in a channel peer crosses as a value, not a raised
exception. The value is a
[`TaskError`](`pymizu.TaskError`) carrying the original exception's
class name as ``remote_type`` and its traceback text as
``detail``; raise it to propagate the error.

Returns
-------
    True for a received remote error, False otherwise.

MizuError

Base class for all pymizu errors.

ShmError

A shared-memory region operation failed. Also an OSError: the failure is at the OS layer. Carries a 'bytes' attribute: the requested size of a region that was not created, None when a region was not opened.

StartupError

A channel peer or pool worker failed to attach within the startup timeout.

SubmitTimeoutError

Pool.submit() timed out waiting for injection-ring space. Also a TimeoutError.

SlotsExhaustedError

Pool.submit() found no free result slot: too many outstanding (uncollected) tasks.

StoppedError

The pool is stopped; no further submission is possible.

CancelledError

The task was cancelled before it ran.

TaskError

The task callable raised. Carries 'remote_type' and 'detail' attributes describing the worker-side exception.

WorkerDiedError

The executing worker died mid-task. Carries 'slot' and 'pid' attributes identifying the worker.

TaskLostError

The task's payload region vanished or could not be read before any worker ran it. No worker died.

DeclinedError

A send on a foreign-language channel of a value outside the portable interchange subset. Carries 'path' and 'reason' attributes ('reason' includes the one-line rewrite guidance for the value).

ForeignPayloadError

A received payload in a language-private or unrecognized format: the peer sent a value outside the portable interchange subset. The message is consumed, so the ring is never blocked, and under recv_async() only the Future waiting on that message rejects.

ConcurrentUseError

A verb ran concurrently with another verb in the same handle role: each handle role is confined to one thread at a time (libmizu 'Handle threading').


## Housekeeping

The process-wide default pool, the current worker's own pool handle, and cleaning up shared memory left by dead processes.


default_pool() -> 'Pool | None'

The process-wide default pool, or None when none is set.

Set with [`set_default_pool()`](`pymizu.set_default_pool`); scoped
use with [`using_pool()`](`pymizu.using_pool`). Package code taking
an optional pool resolves it in this order: an explicit ``pool``
argument, then [`current_pool()`](`pymizu.current_pool`) inside a
task (the evaluating worker's own pool, for nested submission), then
``default_pool()``, then the caller's own fallback, such as sequential
execution or an error.

Setting a default checks only the type: a stopped pool is accepted and
fails at use time with the usual stopped-pool errors. Handles from
[`Pool.attach()`](`pymizu.Pool.attach`) are valid defaults; ownership and
teardown stay with the pool's creator.

The default is process-global: every thread sees the same pool, and
[`current_pool()`](`pymizu.current_pool`) remains the thread-local
mechanism. After a ``fork()``, a child process reads it as unset, because
handles are process-private.

set_default_pool(pool: 'Pool | None') -> 'Pool | None'

Set the process-wide default pool; None clears it.

Returns
-------
    The previous default (a Pool or None), so callers can save and
    restore.

Details
-------
Setting a default keeps the pool alive: it survives even after its
variable is deleted, until the default is cleared or replaced. See
[`default_pool()`](`pymizu.default_pool`) for the full semantics.

using_pool(pool: 'Pool | None') -> '_Generator[Pool | None, None, None]'

Use ``pool`` as the default for the with block, then restore.

Parameters
----------
pool
    The pool to make the default; ``None`` scopes a cleared
    default.

Returns
-------
    A context manager yielding ``pool``. The previous default
    returns on exit, including on exception.

current_pool() -> 'Pool | None'

The pool handle of the worker running the task.

Returns
-------
    The worker's own pool handle inside a task; None outside one.

Details
-------
A task uses it for nested submission: a nested submit goes onto the
worker's own queue, with no ring and no wait, and a nested collect runs
other work instead of sleeping, so nested fan-outs are cheap and cannot
deadlock the pool. The process-wide default set with
[`default_pool()`](`pymizu.default_pool`) never overrides this binding.

current_rng() -> '_np.random.Generator | None'

Return the current element's numpy Generator inside a seeded map.

Returns
-------
    The element's own ``numpy.random.Generator`` inside a seeded map
    element. None outside one.

Raises
------
TypeError
    When numpy is not installed.

Details
-------
The first call in an element creates the generator from the map seed.
Later calls in that element continue the same stream. This derivation is
separate from the stdlib `random` stream. See
[`Pool.map()`](`pymizu.Pool.map`) for the seed format, reproducibility
rules, and nested-task restriction.

prune() -> 'list[str]'

Remove orphaned shared memory regions.

Removes the pymizu shared memory regions that dead processes leave behind.
This is needed only in exceptional circumstances. Cleanup after a crash is
automatic as long as any participant of the pool or channel survives it,
because the survivor detects the death and reclaims the dead process's
regions itself. Orphans arise only when every attached process dies at once
(for example, the whole process group is killed), so no survivor remains to
run that cleanup. They persist until pruned or until the machine reboots.

Regions of running processes are never touched. Do not run this while
another pymizu session on the machine is recovering from a crash: values
sent by a now-dead peer stay readable by its survivor until consumed, and
this function would remove them.

A crashed process cannot clean up after itself, and a new process
that happens to reuse its PID cannot reap its orphans either (it
reads its own PID as alive). Run ``prune()`` while the PID is free,
before reuse.

Returns
-------
    The region names removed, or an empty list if none were. On
    platforms whose shared memory namespace cannot be enumerated
    (Windows, where orphans cannot exist), always an empty list.


----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the User Guide documentation for the package.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Guide

## Requirements

- Python 3.11 or later, on a 64-bit platform.
- Linux: kernel 5.3 or later.
- macOS: 10.15 or later.
- Windows: the build requires clang-cl.

## Install

Install from PyPI:

```sh
pip install pymizu
```

Or the development version from GitHub:

```sh
pip install git+https://github.com/shikokuchuo/pymizu
```

The extension compiles its vendored C core during install, so you need no system libraries.

Optional extras:

- `pymizu[numpy]`: zero-copy array views and raw-tier array staging.
- `pymizu[cloudpickle]`: lambdas, closures, and local functions as pool tasks.

To add an extra to the GitHub install:

```sh
pip install "pymizu[numpy] @ git+https://github.com/shikokuchuo/pymizu"
```

## Deploying on Linux

pymizu detects a peer's death through `pidfd_open`, so it needs Linux kernel 5.3 or later.

On Linux, POSIX shared memory lives in `/dev/shm`, a bounded tmpfs mount.
Everything pymizu creates must fit there: pool and channel regions, plus the regions that carry larger payloads.
Container runtimes default it to 64 MB; raise it with `docker run --shm-size=4g` or the equivalent in your orchestrator, sized to your peak in-flight payload traffic.

## Linux memory allocator

This section applies only to Linux with glibc.

When pymizu starts a channel peer or a pool worker, that process raises the C allocator's mmap threshold to 32 MB and its trim threshold to 128 MB.
This keeps large payloads in fast memory.
Without it, glibc asks the kernel to map and unmap each large payload, which is slow.

Your own Python process is unchanged.
To get the same settings there, set them before Python starts:

```sh
export GLIBC_TUNABLES=glibc.malloc.mmap_threshold=33554432:glibc.malloc.trim_threshold=134217728
```

If you set `GLIBC_TUNABLES` yourself, pymizu respects your values.


### Benchmarks

These tables measure task-communication overhead against the stdlib `concurrent.futures` pools, on an Apple M4 Pro (`benchmarks/mizu-stdlib-bench.py`).

First, `ProcessPoolExecutor`: tasks run in separate processes, and every payload crosses as a pickle.

| Benchmark | pymizu | ProcessPoolExecutor | Speedup |
|----|----|----|----|
| Trivial task round trip | 0.6 µs | 94.2 µs | 157x |
| Pipelined throughput, 1 worker | 2,390,000 tasks/s | 18,500 tasks/s | 129x |
| 8 KB vector round trip | 2.4 µs | 100.7 µs | 42x |
| Parallel map of 2,000 ~5 µs tasks, 4 workers | 2.9 ms | 123 ms | 42x |

Next, `ThreadPoolExecutor`: tasks share one process, so the GIL caps CPU-bound work at one core.

| Benchmark | pymizu | ThreadPoolExecutor | Speedup |
|----|----|----|----|
| Trivial task round trip | 0.6 µs | 9.5 µs | 16x |
| Pipelined throughput, 1 worker | 2,390,000 tasks/s | 405,000 tasks/s | 5.9x |
| 8 KB vector round trip | 2.4 µs | 9.3 µs | 3.9x |
| Parallel map of 2,000 ~5 µs tasks, 4 workers | 2.9 ms | 48 ms | 17x |

## How pymizu compares

pymizu runs processes in parallel on one machine and moves data through shared memory instead of pickled copies.
The tools below overlap at the edges; they differ in what has to run, how data moves, and what survives a crash.

| Tool | What runs | How data moves | Best for |
|----|----|----|----|
| `multiprocessing`<br>`concurrent.futures` | Stdlib only | Pickle copies per task | Coarse tasks, maximum portability |
| `joblib` | Reusable worker pool (loky) | Pickle; large arrays memmapped to disk | Coarse parallel loops anywhere |
| `ipyparallel` | Controller + engines | Pickle over ZeroMQ | Interactive use from Jupyter |
| Ray | Scheduler, object store, dashboard | Zero-copy object store (one node) | Cluster scaling, actors, GPU placement |
| Dask | Scheduler (+ `distributed` workers) | Process copies; threads share heap | Out-of-core dataframes and arrays |
| Free-threaded CPython | Threads | Zero copies — shared heap | CPU work, no isolation needed |
| `concurrent.interpreters` | Stdlib only (3.14+) | Builtins copy, buffers share; no numpy | Process-free isolation |
| pymizu | A library | Shared-memory views, µs handoff | Fine-grained tasks, large arrays, R interop |

### Process pools: `multiprocessing`, `concurrent.futures`, joblib, ipyparallel

The stdlib pools are the baseline in the tables above.

joblib's `Parallel`/`delayed` is the standard tool for embarrassingly parallel loops over numpy data.
Its `loky` backend is the most similar to pymizu: a reusable process pool that memmaps large arrays to a temp folder instead of pickling them.
That avoids the pickle copy, but the array still round-trips through the filesystem, and a task round trip stays in the millisecond range.

ipyparallel brings process pools to Jupyter: a controller process brokers pickled messages over ZeroMQ sockets to engine processes.
That generality costs a controller in the loop and a socket copy per message.

`multiprocessing.shared_memory` gives you raw shared buffers and leaves synchronization, lifetime tracking, and crash cleanup to you.
pymizu builds on the same idea — the same pages — and adds the waiting, framing, and peer-death detection.

### Distributed frameworks: Ray and Dask

Ray and Dask spread work across machines.
On one machine, that design has a cost: a local Ray instance still starts a scheduler, an object store, and a dashboard, and a task round trip costs on the order of a millisecond.

Dask's `distributed` scheduler is similar; its threaded scheduler shares memory, but the GIL caps it for Python-level work.
Ray's object store does read numpy arrays without copying on one node.
The difference on one machine is overhead and footprint.

### Modern CPython: free-threading and subinterpreters

Python 3.14 officially supports a free-threaded build with the GIL removed: threads share one heap and exchange data with no copies at all.
If you do not need isolation, it is the best tool for single-language CPU parallelism.
The tradeoffs: a crashing thread takes the process down, C extensions must be built and validated for it, and it does not cross into R.
pymizu targets the standard GIL build and does not yet support free-threading.
The two approaches solve different problems: threads trade isolation for sharing; pymizu keeps the isolation and makes the sharing cheap.

Python 3.14 also added `concurrent.interpreters` to the stdlib ([PEP 734](https://peps.python.org/pep-0734/)): multiple interpreters in one process, each with its own GIL, so CPU work parallelizes without new processes on the standard build.
Objects that cross between interpreters must be shareable: builtin scalars and plain containers copy across, buffer-protocol objects share their memory (synchronization is on you), and everything else — numpy arrays included — is rejected.
The isolation is real but not OS-level: a fatal error in one interpreter ends the process, and you build the surrounding machinery (queues, lifetimes, crash handling) yourself.
`concurrent.interpreters` requires Python 3.14+; pymizu runs on 3.11+.

### R workers

Only pymizu can run a pool of R workers, exchanging numpy arrays, polars DataFrames, and Arrow tables as shared-memory views (see [R interop](interop.qmd)).
No other tool here crosses the language boundary.

- Choose pymizu when the work fits one machine and tasks are fine-grained, data is large, or you need R.
- Choose Ray or Dask when you outgrow one machine.
- Choose `concurrent.interpreters` for stdlib-only isolation when you can require Python 3.14.
- Choose free-threading when one language and shared-everything is acceptable.

To reproduce these numbers, run `benchmarks/mizu-bench.py` (pymizu standalone), `benchmarks/mizu-stdlib-bench.py` (the comparison above), or `benchmarks/crosslang-map-bench.py` (the cross-language map comparison).
The scripts report timings but assert nothing about them — CI runner timing is too variable — and dated records live in `benchmarks/notes.md`.


### Channels

A channel is a two-way message link between your Python process and a helper process it spawns: one lock-free ring per direction, over shared memory.
One side writes into shared memory and the other reads it in place — no copies through sockets, pipes, or files.

## Creating a channel

`Channel.create()` spawns the peer process and connects both ends.
Pass the peer program as a Python source string; the peer evaluates it with `ch` bound to its side of the channel:

```{python}
import pymizu

ch = pymizu.Channel.create("""
import pymizu
while True:
    x = ch.recv()
    if x is pymizu.CLOSED:
        break
    ch.send(x)
""")
```

The peer is a full Python process: it can import anything your interpreter can.
`Channel.create()` waits up to `startup_timeout` seconds for the peer to connect and raises `StartupError` on expiry.

A `launcher` changes how the peer spawns: one callable that takes the channel's token and starts the peer process.
The built-in `pymizu.r_launcher()` spawns an R peer (see [R interop](interop.qmd)); write your own to spawn peers any other way.

## Sending and receiving

`ch.send()` publishes a value, and the peer can see it as soon as the call returns.
Sends never block for ring space.
`ch.recv()` returns the next value, waiting up to `timeout` seconds (indefinitely when omitted):

```{python}
ch.send([1, "a", None])
ch.recv(timeout=5)
```

Outcomes that end a conversation come back as sentinel singletons, not exceptions:

| Sentinel | Returned when |
|---|---|
| `pymizu.FULL` | a send finds the ring full |
| `pymizu.TIMEOUT` | a receive's timeout expires |
| `pymizu.CLOSED` | the peer has closed and the ring is drained |
| `pymizu.PEER_GONE` | the peer process has died and the ring is drained |

Test for them by identity (`x is pymizu.TIMEOUT`) or with `pymizu.is_sentinel(x)` — no call needs an error handler.
If the peer dies, receives drain what it already sent, then report `PEER_GONE`.

When per-call overhead starts to matter, `send_batch()` and `recv_batch()` move several values in one call:

```{python}
ch.send_batch(range(4))
ch.recv_batch(4, timeout=5)
```

`ch.alive()` reports whether the peer still runs, without touching the rings.
`ch.info()` returns a read-only snapshot of the channel's state.

## asyncio

For event-driven receives, `ch.recv_async()` returns an `asyncio.Future` that resolves with the next value when it arrives — no blocking, no polling.
It takes no timeout; use `asyncio.timeout` or `asyncio.wait_for`.
Terminal states stay values: the Future resolves with `CLOSED` or `PEER_GONE`.
Outstanding calls resolve in call order, one message each.
Cancelling a Future detaches its waiter and passes the next message to the one behind it.
When arrivals come in bursts, `ch.recv_batch_async(n)` resolves one Future with up to `n` values as one list — short when fewer have arrived, never waiting to fill — the high-throughput receive form.

```{python}
ch.send(1)
assert await ch.recv_async() == 1
ch.send(2)
await ch.recv_async()
```

```{python}
ch.send_batch([3, 4])
await ch.recv_batch_async()
```

`async for x in ch` is the stream form: it awaits each value through `recv_async()` and ends on `CLOSED` or `PEER_GONE`, as the sync iterator does.

A message outside the portable interchange subset (a language-private stream from the peer) is declined at read time with `ForeignPayloadError`; the message is consumed and the channel keeps flowing.
Under `recv_async()`, only that message's waiter rejects.
The rejection also ends an `async for` loop, and a try/except inside the loop body cannot catch it — wrap the whole loop and re-enter on the same channel to skip the message.

## Closing

`ch.close()` is the orderly shutdown: it tells the peer to close and waits for it to finish reading before releasing the shared memory:

```{python}
ch.close()
```

A channel is also a context manager: the `with` block closes it on exit.
`destroy()` skips the wait and releases the handle immediately; the peer sees the channel as closed (`PEER_GONE` if it died hard).
Destroy is safe from any thread: a verb still running on another thread keeps the handle alive until it returns, and a waiting verb (`recv()`, `recv_batch()`, `ready_wait()`, `close()`) wakes promptly so teardown can finish.

## Threading

Each channel side belongs to one thread at a time — libmizu's threading contract, since the shared structures carry no locks by design.
Call a side's verbs (`send()`, `recv()`, their batch forms, `ready_wait()`) from one thread only; a second verb from another thread raises `ConcurrentUseError` instead of corrupting the ring.
The guard is a check, not a lock: it never waits, it reports the mistake.
Blocking receives and `recv_async()` are likewise exclusive on a side: a blocking receive while async receives are pending raises `ConcurrentUseError` at the call site, except on the async consumer's own event-loop thread, whose receives can never race it.
For two-way traffic from two threads, use two channels (one per direction, each on its own thread) or route every call through a single thread.
`destroy()` is the exception: it is safe from any thread, as described in Closing.

## What crosses a channel

pymizu chooses the cheapest transport for each value:

1. `None` crosses as a marker: no data moves.
2. Buffer-protocol objects (`bytes`, 1-D C-contiguous numpy arrays) cross without serialization.
   float64, int32, int64, complex128, and uint8 keep their exact values and arrive as arrays (`bytes` arrives as a uint8 array).
   numpy scalars and 0-d arrays keep their exact type and shape.
   A large buffer arrives as a read-only zero-copy view over the shared pages, with no copy and no parse.
   A contiguous buffer below 256 KB instead crosses as one copy into shared memory, which is cheaper than a separate region at those sizes.
   From 256 KB the receive is a view.
3. A `str` that fits in a slot crosses as raw UTF-8.
4. Booleans, numbers, and flat lists or dicts of them cross in a compact binary form.
5. Everything else crosses as a pickle (protocol 4).

Each end of a channel knows the peer's language.
Between two Python processes it changes nothing: arrays of the listed dtypes cross unchanged, and everything else pickles.
An R peer restricts values to a portable subset both languages share; a value outside it raises `pymizu.DeclinedError` at send time, naming the value and the reason, and the channel stays usable.
See [R interop](interop.qmd).

An uncaught error in the peer crosses as a value, not a raised exception: a `pymizu.TaskError` carrying the original class name and traceback text.
Test a received value with `pymizu.is_remote_error(x)`; raise it to propagate the error.

## Frames without pickling

Between two Python processes, a pyarrow `Table`, polars `DataFrame`, or duckdb relation pickles by default — type-exact, but a full serialize-and-parse round trip.
`pymizu.Frame.from_arrow()` sends an Arrow producer as a frame instead: one shared-memory region, read in place at receive.
Here the peer sums a 200,000-row column straight off the shared pages — only the small result crosses back:

```{python}
import pyarrow as pa

with pymizu.Channel.create("""
import pymizu
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.compute as pc

while True:
    f = ch.recv()
    if f is pymizu.CLOSED:
        break
    t = pa.table(f)
    ch.send(pc.sum(t.column("x")).as_py())
""") as ch:
    f = pymizu.Frame.from_arrow(
        pa.table({"x": pa.array([1.5, None] * 100_000)})
    )
    ch.send(f)
    result = ch.recv(timeout=5)
result
```

The peer's `pa.table(f)` borrows the region's buffers, so the sum runs where the data already lives.

Construction adopts the producer's own buffers wherever the column layout is already the Arrow layout: a single-batch producer on offset-0 boundaries, nulls included (the validity bitmap is adopted with the values).
It copies only what it must:

| Stage | Copies |
|---|---|
| producer → `Frame.from_arrow()` | 0 per adopted column; a per-column copy only where its type forces it |
| `ch.send(f)` | 1 — the layout write into the shared region (the region is the wire) |
| `ch.recv()` | 0 — the frame reads the region in place |
| `pa.table(f)` | 0 — the frame's `__arrow_c_stream__` exports borrowed buffers |

Values cross exactly, but types normalize.
A column whose type forces a copy is copied rather than declined:

| In | Out (the received frame's Arrow export) |
|---|---|
| `string` | `large_string` |
| `string_view` | `large_string` (copies) |
| `bool` | `bool` (copies: bit-packed) |
| int8 / int16 / uint16 | int32 (copies) |
| uint32 / half_float / float32 | float64 (copies) |
| uint64 | uint64 (adopts) |
| timestamp[s / ms / us / ns] | timestamp[s / ms / us / ns] (adopts) |
| duration[s / ms / us / ns] | duration[s / ms / us / ns] (adopts) |
| dictionary\<i32, utf8\> | dictionary\<i32, string\> (adopts; other index widths copy) |
| chunked or sliced columns | concatenated or rebased (copies) |

Chunked pyarrow tables adopt after `table.combine_chunks()`.
Timestamps and durations keep their counts and unit: a `timestamp[ns]` round trip is exact to the nanosecond, timezone included.
Nanosecond precision needs this pymizu version on both ends; an older peer (or R) receives the microsecond form instead, values rounded to the wire format's microsecond precision, with no error.

Adopted buffers stay alive for the frame's lifetime: a frame built from a 4 GB table keeps the whole table in memory, like a numpy view.
`to_dict()`'s masked reads copy where the Arrow export does not.
When you want the exact producer type back, keep the default: a plain pyarrow or polars object pickles and comes back type-exact.
On a pool, a `Frame` task argument and a frame returned from a task both ride the shared-memory region as on a channel (see [the pools guide](pools.qmd#frames-as-task-arguments)).
`Pool.map` does not accept a frame as its element source.

## Sizing

`Channel.create()` takes `capacity` (ring slots, a power of two), `slot_size` (bytes per slot, so a payload of up to `slot_size - 16` bytes fits in a slot), and `arena_size` (the channel's shared staging area).
A value too large for a slot goes to the staging area or a fresh shared-memory region.
`spin=True` makes receivers busy-wait instead of sleeping: the lowest latency, at full CPU while waiting.


### Task pools

A pool is a set of worker processes that share out submitted tasks.
`Pool.create()` spawns them.
Workers pull tasks from per-submitter queues and steal work from each other, so the load balances itself.
A submission costs one shared-memory write plus at most one wake-up — there is no dispatcher process.

```{python}
import pymizu

with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    task = pool.submit(pow, 2, 16)
    result = task.collect(timeout=5)

result
```

`pool.submit()` returns a `Task` handle immediately, and `task.collect()` waits for the result.
The pool is a context manager: leaving the block stops it.
`pool.stop()` cancels the pending tasks, waits for the workers to exit cleanly, and releases the shared memory.
The pool lives only as long as its creating process; dropping the handle shuts it down without waiting for the workers.

## Task callables

A task callable travels by pickle, so under the standard pickle it must be an importable reference, as with `multiprocessing`; installing cloudpickle lifts that restriction.
Task arguments follow the same rules as [channel values](channels.qmd#what-crosses-a-channel): a buffer-protocol argument larger than 32 KB arrives as a read-only view over the shared pages, not a writable copy.

## Frames as task arguments

A [`Frame`](`pymizu.Frame`) argument follows the same rule: past the size floor it crosses as one shared-memory region, and the worker's callable reads it in place, as on a channel.
Below the floor it pickles (the worker gets a copy), as it does with a complex column, which has no Arrow type.
Only one region crosses per task: a second region-sized argument (another frame or a large buffer) moves the whole task to pickle, values exact.
Raw pyarrow and polars frames stay on the pickle path and round-trip with their exact types — construct the `Frame` first to use the shared region instead.

## Outcomes

| Outcome | On collect |
|---|---|
| The task raised | `pymizu.TaskError`, with `remote_type` and `detail` |
| The task was cancelled before it ran | `pymizu.CancelledError` |
| The executing worker died | `pymizu.WorkerDiedError`, with `slot` and `pid` |
| The task's payload region vanished before any worker ran it | `pymizu.TaskLostError` |
| The collect timeout expired | the `pymizu.TIMEOUT` sentinel |

A task error crosses as a plain description (type, message, traceback), not a pickled exception object.
The OS reports a worker's death immediately — no heartbeats, no polling.
Only the tasks the dead worker had claimed fail; the surviving workers take over the rest of its queue.

`task.cancel()` withdraws a task: a queued task is skipped, a running one completes and its result is discarded.
Cancellation never interrupts executing code.

Submission itself can fail: `SubmitTimeoutError` when the submit queue stays full past `timeout`, `SlotsExhaustedError` when too many tasks are outstanding and uncollected, `StoppedError` on a stopped pool.

## Waiting on several tasks

`pool.collect_any()` waits on a list of task handles and returns `(index, value)` for the first to finish; the other handles stay collectible.
`pool.collect_all()` returns every value in input order once all have finished.
Both take one overall `timeout` and return the `TIMEOUT` sentinel on expiry, consuming nothing:

```{python}
import time

with pymizu.Pool.create(2) as pool:
    tasks = [pool.submit(time.sleep, 0.5), pool.submit(len, "pymizu")]
    first = pool.collect_any(tasks, timeout=5)

first
```

```{python}
with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    tasks = [pool.submit(pow, 2, i) for i in range(4)]
    rest = pool.collect_all(tasks, timeout=5)

rest
```

`pool.submit_batch()` submits one task per zero-argument callable in a single call.
Bind arguments with `functools.partial`.

## asyncio

For event-driven collects, `await task` (or `task.collect_async()`) returns an `asyncio.Future` that resolves with the result — or raises the task's error — when it arrives, with no blocking and no polling.
Cancelling the Future only detaches the waiter: a later blocking `collect()` works again, and the task itself is never cancelled (only `task.cancel()` does that).
Each result has one consumer: a task with a pending async collect refuses blocking collects.

`pool.collect_any_async(tasks)` and `pool.collect_all_async(tasks)` are the batch forms: one Future per collection, re-checked whenever a task finishes, otherwise behaving like the sync verbs.
Collect-all resolves in input order and rejects the first error by position with its `index`; collect-any resolves `(index, value)` for the first task to finish.
Neither takes a timeout — use `asyncio.timeout` or `asyncio.wait_for`.

```{python}
with pymizu.Pool.create(2) as pool:
    tasks = [pool.submit(pow, 2, i) for i in range(4)]
    rest = await pool.collect_all_async(tasks)

rest
```

`await pool.map(fn, x)` resolves a map handle the same way (see [Parallel map](map.qmd)).

## Nested tasks

Inside a task, `pymizu.current_pool()` returns the pool handle of the worker running it.
A nested submit lands on that worker's own queue — no ring, no wake-up — and a worker waiting on a nested result runs other work instead of sleeping.
Recursive fan-out is cheap and cannot deadlock the pool:

```{python}
def fan_out(parts):
    pool = pymizu.current_pool()
    subs = [pool.submit(sum, part) for part in parts]
    return sum(t.collect() for t in subs)

parts = [range(0, 250), range(250, 500), range(500, 750), range(750, 1000)]

with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    total = pool.submit(fan_out, parts).collect()

total
```

(This example needs cloudpickle: `fan_out` is not an importable reference.)

`Pool.map()` nests the same way: a task can map over its own pool.
See [Nested maps](map.qmd#nested-maps).

## A default pool for package code

Package code can read a process-wide default pool with `pymizu.default_pool()`.
`pymizu.set_default_pool(pool)` sets it (`None` clears it) and returns the previous default, so you can save and restore.
A pool set as the default stays alive after its variable is deleted.
`pymizu.using_pool(pool)` scopes the default to a `with` block, restoring the previous default on exit, exception included.

Resolve an optional pool in this order: an explicit `pool` argument, `current_pool()` inside a task, `default_pool()`, then your own fallback (sequential execution or an error).
Inside a task, `current_pool()` takes precedence over the default, so nested submission always goes to the worker's own pool.
Setting a default checks only the type: a stopped pool is accepted and fails when used.
Handles from `Pool.attach()` are valid defaults.

```{python}
def run(x, pool=None):
    pool = pool or pymizu.current_pool() or pymizu.default_pool()
    if pool is None:
        raise RuntimeError("no pool: pass one, or set a default")
    return pool.submit(pow, x, 2).collect(timeout=30)

with pymizu.Pool.create(2) as pool:
    old = pymizu.set_default_pool(pool)
    squared = run(21)
    pymizu.set_default_pool(old)

squared
```

## Growing, shrinking, and joining a pool

A pool can grow and shrink while it runs.
`pool.spawn_workers(n)` adds workers, up to the `max_workers` limit set at create.
`pool.retire(slot)` asks a worker to exit cleanly: it finishes its current task, and the remaining workers take over anything still queued to it.
Only the creator resizes a pool; an attached submitter gets `MizuError`.

Other processes join a running pool as submitters with `Pool.attach(token)`, where the token is the creator's `pool.token`.
Attached submitters submit and collect exactly as the creator does.

## Observing a pool

Four read-only tools watch a running pool without disturbing it:

```python
pool.info()   # snapshot: worker states, queued tasks, result slots
pool.stats()    # cumulative counters since each participant joined
pool.dump()     # every slot in full detail; start here when a pool hangs
pool.trace(fn)  # fn(event, id) at each task lifecycle event; None removes it
```

## Threading

A pool handle is single-producer: call its submit family (`submit()`, `submit_batch()`, `map()`) from one thread only.
A second concurrent producer raises `ConcurrentUseError` instead of corrupting the submission queue.
The guard is a check, not a lock: it never waits, it reports the mistake.
The waiting half (the blocking collects, `ready_wait()`, `stop()`) likewise belongs to one thread — which may differ from the producer's — and a concurrent second wait raises the same error.
This is libmizu's threading contract: the shared structures carry no locks by design.

Three ways to produce from several threads, in rough order of preference:

1. `PoolExecutor`: its `submit()` is thread-safe through an internal lock, and it resolves futures as results arrive (see the next section).
2. Funnel submissions through one thread, for example `run_in_executor` with a single-worker `ThreadPoolExecutor`, while collects stay on their own thread.
3. `Pool.attach(token)` one handle per thread: each attached handle is its own producer with its own submission queue.

Avoid `asyncio.to_thread(pool.submit, ...)` from concurrent coroutines: the default executor is multi-threaded, so the submits race and raise `ConcurrentUseError`.
`destroy()` is the one verb that is safe from any thread, as with channels.

## concurrent.futures interop

`pymizu.PoolExecutor` adapts a pool to the stdlib `concurrent.futures.Executor` interface, so code written against `ProcessPoolExecutor` drops in: `submit` returns real `concurrent.futures.Future` objects, and `wait`, `as_completed`, `asyncio.wrap_future`, and chunked `map` all work unchanged.
Futures resolve as results arrive, with no background thread and no polling.

```{python}
with pymizu.PoolExecutor.create(4) as ex:
    futures = [ex.submit(pow, 2, i) for i in range(4)]
    result = [f.result() for f in futures]

result
```

Wrap an existing pool with `PoolExecutor(pool)`; its lifetime stays with its owner.
`PoolExecutor.create(workers, **pool_kwargs)` instead spawns an owned pool that `shutdown` stops.
A task's failure surfaces as `pymizu.TaskError`, and cancellation behaves like `Task.cancel`.
If the result table is full, `submit` waits for the executor to collect a result instead of raising `SlotsExhaustedError`; a submit from a listener-thread done callback still raises rather than deadlocking the drain.
The executor's `map` honors `chunksize` and `buffersize` like `ProcessPoolExecutor`; its default remains one task per element, and `Pool.map` remains the faster bulk-map path.

## Sizing a pool

`Pool.create()` sizing options: `max_workers` (the worker limit), `max_submitters`, `injection_cap` (each submitter's queue size), `per_worker_cap` (each worker's queue size), `result_slots` (outstanding uncollected tasks per submitter), and `slot_size` (bytes per queue entry and result slot; a larger payload travels in its own shared-memory region).


### Parallel map

`Pool.map(fn, x)` maps `fn` over `x` on the pool and returns a `Map` handle immediately: setup and submission happen at the call, and you collect results from the handle.
A map is not a loop over `pool.submit()`: the function, its constant `args=`/`kwargs=`, and the data are written to shared memory once, and one *runner* task per worker divides up the elements:

```{python}
import pymizu

with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    result = pool.map(abs, range(-5, 5)).collect()

result
```

## The `Map` handle

A map collects exactly once, through the handle:

- `handle.collect(timeout=None)` blocks for the results: a list in input order, or with `template=` the gathered output area (a view with `collect="view"`). On `timeout` expiry the outstanding work is cancelled and you get the `TIMEOUT` sentinel, not an exception.
- `handle.collect_async()`, or `await handle`, resolves one `asyncio.Future` with the same results when they arrive, with no blocking or polling. Cancelling the Future only detaches the waiter: the handle can be collected blocking again, and the map is never cancelled. A streaming map (`stream=True`) can only be collected blocking, because its sliding task window advances in the blocking collect loop.
- `handle.cancel()` stops the run: workers halt within about one batch, and a pending collect, blocking or async, ends with `CancelledError`.

`Pool.map()`'s own `timeout=` bounds submission only: on its expiry the tasks already in are cancelled and `Pool.map()` itself returns the `TIMEOUT` sentinel (no handle).
A dropped uncollected handle cancels at garbage collection, so no work is wasted.

## Scheduling

Each runner claims batches of elements from a shared counter, and the batch size adapts: a cheap `fn` runs in large batches at near-zero scheduling cost, while an expensive or uneven one takes smaller batches to keep workers balanced.
`n_chunks=` sets the batch size directly.

A 1-D C-contiguous numpy array of float64, int32, int64, complex128, or uint8 crosses as raw bytes.
Each worker views the same array in shared memory and reads its elements directly, so `x` is never serialized:

```{python}
import numpy as np

with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    result = pool.map(np.negative, np.arange(-5.0, 5.0)).collect()

result
```

## Unpacked elements (starmap)

`pool.starmap(fn, x)` unpacks each element of `x` as the call's positional arguments: `fn(*element, *args, **kwargs)`.
This is the `multiprocessing.Pool.starmap` convention:

```{python}
with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    result = pool.starmap(pow, [(2, 10), (3, 3)]).collect()

result
```

For the multi-iterable shape of `concurrent.futures.Executor.map`, zip the iterables first: `pool.starmap(fn, zip(xs, ys))`.
Starmap needs Python workers: a `pymizu.call` spec raises `TypeError`.
Everything else (seeding, templates, streaming, the outcomes) works as in `Pool.map`.

## Reproducible randomness

`seed=` (an int or bytes) gives every element its own deterministic stream of the stdlib `random` module.
Element `i` is seeded from SHA-256 of the seed and `i`.
Results are identical for any chunking, worker count, or steal order:

```{python}
import random

def draw(i):
    return random.random()

with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    a = pool.map(draw, range(100), seed=123).collect()
    b = pool.map(draw, range(100), seed=123, n_chunks=10).collect()
    print(a == b)
```

Pass `seed=(seed, offset)` to shift every element's stream by `offset` positions, for maps split across runs or processes.

`seed=` covers the stdlib `random` module only.
To draw from numpy, call `pymizu.current_rng()` inside the task: the element's own `numpy.random.Generator`, derived from the same seed and created once per element:

```{python}
def draw_np(i):
    return pymizu.current_rng().random()

with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    a = pool.map(draw_np, range(100), seed=123).collect()
    b = pool.map(draw_np, range(100), seed=123, n_chunks=10).collect()
    print(a == b)
```

The legacy `np.random.*` functions draw from the worker's shared global `RandomState`; a seeded map does not make them deterministic, and other RNG libraries (torch, jax) are out of scope.
Also, a seeded map element must not submit and collect nested tasks: while a worker waits for nested results it runs other work — possibly another map's batches mid-element — which can wipe the element's `current_rng()` stash.
The stdlib streams survive.

## Templates

A `template=` example buffer (for example `np.empty(m, dtype=...)`) declares that every `fn` result is `m` values of that dtype.
Workers write results directly into a shared `n x m` output area, so each result crosses the process boundary once, with no serialization.
Each result must be a matching buffer; when `m == 1`, a plain Python scalar also works:

```{python}
import math

with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    result = pool.map(math.log1p, [1.0, 2.0, 3.0], template=np.empty(1)).collect()

result
```

With a template, `collect="copy"` (the default) returns the output as one numpy array of shape `(n, m)` — `(n,)` when `m == 1` — or a memoryview when numpy is not installed.
`collect="view"` returns the shared output area itself as a read-only zero-copy view, released when the view is garbage-collected.
The view exports `__arrow_c_array__`, so an Arrow consumer such as pyarrow or polars wraps it without numpy.
With numpy, reach the view through the result's `.base` (`arr.base` when `m == 1`, one link deeper when `m > 1`); without numpy, it is `mv.obj` on the memoryview.

## Streaming maps

With `stream=True`, the map does not write the whole of `x` to shared memory; it streams slices to workers as they take work.
Slices travel as ordinary chunk tasks under a sliding submit/collect window: at most `min(n_chunks, 2 * live workers, free result slots)` tasks stay outstanding, so shared-memory use is bounded by `window x slice` instead of `sizeof(x)`.
The chunk count defaults to `min(len(x), 32 * live workers)`; `n_chunks=` overrides it.

```{python}
with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    result = pool.map(abs, range(-5, 5), stream=True).collect()

result
```

Everything else (ordering, `template=` and `collect=`, `seed=` reproducibility, the errors) works as in the non-streaming map.
Fixed chunks have two costs: the adaptive batch sizing is lost (raise `n_chunks=` to reduce skew), and slices are serialized like ordinary task payloads, so each chunk pays a submit's serialization cost instead of the zero-copy path a raw array gets.
A streaming map with Python workers shares one description of the map with every worker, each read at most once.
A `pymizu.call` spec as `fn` streams too, over workers of any language.
Each chunk in the window writes its own small shared-memory region — the slice plus the task that runs it, one runner per chunk — removed as soon as the chunk completes, so shared-memory use stays bounded by the window plus a small per-worker cache rather than `sizeof(x)`.
Each chunk also writes its results separately, so they cannot combine into one view: `collect="view"` raises `TypeError` on a streaming spec map, as does preparing one with `pool.map_prepare()`.

## Prepared maps

`pool.map_prepare()` stages a map once for repeated runs: the data is written to shared memory once, and each worker sets up the map once.
Each `m.run()` then costs only the task submissions and the collection, reuses each worker's cached setup, and returns the run's handle:

```{python}
with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    with pool.map_prepare(abs, range(-5, 5)) as m:
        print(m.run().collect())
        print(m.run().collect())
```

`m.run(x=...)` replaces the data for that and later runs: a raw-array replacement of the same dtype and length copies over the old data in place; anything else is written out fresh.
A streaming prepared map keeps `x` on the submitter, so a replacement of any shape re-slices.
Only a length change under `template=` uses fresh shared memory, as does the run after one collected with `collect="view"` (the previous output area belongs to the returned view).
`m.run(seed=...)` reseeds the run's element streams and `m.run(collect=...)` chooses the result form — both per-run options, because the seed travels with the run's tasks rather than the staged data.

## Nested maps

Maps nest: a task can start a map on its worker's own pool handle, via `pymizu.current_pool()`.
The runner submissions land on the worker's own queue, and while the worker waits it runs its own runners while idle workers steal the rest — a nested map cannot deadlock the pool.

```{python}
def nested_total(parts):
    return sum(pymizu.current_pool().map(sum, parts).collect())

parts = [range(0, 250), range(250, 500), range(500, 750), range(750, 1000)]

with pymizu.Pool.create(4) as pool:
    total = pool.submit(nested_total, parts).collect()

total
```

(This example needs cloudpickle: `nested_total` is not an importable reference.)

A worker's first nested map claims a submitter slot.
The default `max_submitters = 8` holds one slot for the creating process, so at most 7 workers can nest concurrently; raise `max_submitters` for wider fan-outs.
Do not nest inside the element of a seeded map — while a worker waits for nested results it runs other work, possibly another map's batches mid-element, which can wipe the element's `current_rng()` stash.
See [Reproducible randomness](#reproducible-randomness).

## Outcomes

- An error raised by `fn` re-raises as `pymizu.TaskError` carrying the failing element's 0-based `index`.
  The map fails fast: the workers stop within about one batch.
- Worker death raises `pymizu.WorkerDiedError` carrying the lost element ranges as `lost` (0-based half-open `(lo, hi)` pairs, possibly wider than what was lost).
- On `timeout=` expiry the outstanding work is cancelled and the `pymizu.TIMEOUT` sentinel is returned, not raised.
- Ctrl-C during a map cancels its outstanding tasks.

A map started inside a task runs on the worker's own pool handle via `pymizu.current_pool()`; a `pymizu.call` spec as `fn` is the cross-language map (see [R interop](interop.qmd#mapping-over-a-foreign-pool)).


### R interop

The process at the other end of a channel does not have to be Python.
[mizu](https://github.com/shikokuchuo/mizu) is pymizu's R counterpart, built on the same shared-memory core, and a channel or pool connects the two languages as directly as two Python processes.

## R channel peers

A channel peer can be an R process with the `mizu` package installed: pass the peer program as R source and set the launcher to `pymizu.r_launcher()`.
Here, an R process doubles the array you send:

```python
import numpy as np
import pymizu

ch = pymizu.Channel.create(
    """
library(mizu)
repeat {
  x <- mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 30)
  if (inherits(x, "mizu_sentinel")) break
  mizu_send(ch, x * 2)
}
""",
    launcher=pymizu.r_launcher(),
)

ch.send(np.array([1.5, 2.5, 3.5]))
print(ch.recv(timeout=5))            # [3. 5. 7.]
ch.close()
```

`r_launcher()` needs R and the `mizu` package installed; if either is missing it raises `MizuError` before the channel exists.
Pass `rscript=` to use a specific R installation.

The reverse direction works too — an R session spawns a Python peer with `mizu::mizu_py_launcher()`.

## Large data crosses without copying

Above a size threshold, pymizu writes the data to shared memory once and both sides read it in place — nothing is serialized, parsed, or copied again.
R reads a large value you send directly over the shared pages; a large value you receive arrives as a view over those pages, usually wrapped as a numpy array.
The peer below echoes back whatever it receives; this channel stays open for the next few examples:

```python
ch = pymizu.Channel.create(
    """
library(mizu)
repeat {
  x <- mizu_recv(ch, timeout = 30)
  if (inherits(x, "mizu_sentinel")) break
  mizu_send(ch, x)
}
""",
    launcher=pymizu.r_launcher(),
)

big = np.random.default_rng(0).normal(size=1_250_000)  # ten megabytes
ch.send(big)
back = ch.recv(timeout=5)
np.array_equal(back, big)                              # True
```

Apart from the one write into the shared region, no data moved: R's echo came back as a reference, with no payload bytes.
Send a received view onward and it crosses the same way, as the region's name alone.
Zero-copy covers every large layout: a flat array of an exact-match dtype (`float64`, `int32`, `int64`, `complex128`, `uint8`), an array of any shape and memory order, a nested tree of lists, dicts, arrays, and strings, a `datetime64` array (`NaT` crosses as `NA`), or a `list[str | None]` (`None` crosses as `NA`).
A large data frame crosses as one shared region in both directions.
The floor is 256 KB for a flat contiguous array on a channel, 32 KB everywhere else.[^byvalue]

Arrays of other numeric dtypes (booleans, the narrow ints, `uint64`, `float32`, ...) cross as a converted copy at any size; the [dtype matrix](#the-dtype-matrix) has the per-dtype rule.
Without numpy, a received view is a plain buffer: `memoryview(view)` works, and `pa.array(view)` or `pl.from_arrow(view)` wrap the same pages without copying.
One exception: R's ALTREP vectors (such as `1:1e9`, stored as a recipe rather than data) cross by value, values exact.
A polars or pyarrow object that wraps a received frame keeps the frame's region alive until garbage collection, so delete these wrappers when you no longer need them.

[^byvalue]: Below the floor, a value crosses as one quick copy.
    At any size, these types cross: Python scalars (`bool`, `int`, `float`, `complex`, `str`, `None`), lists, dicts with `str` keys (a tuple arrives as a `list` in R), `bytes` (an R raw vector), and `datetime.date` / `datetime.datetime` scalars (length-1 dates and times in R).
    A few round trips change the container but not the values: a standalone R factor comes back as strings, a length-1 `NA` arrives as `None` and sent back is R's `NULL`, and a standalone `POSIXct` normalizes to UTC (the instant is exact).

## What crosses

Small values round-trip exactly too.
Each form below comes back from R unchanged:

```python
def echo(x):
    ch.send(x)
    return ch.recv(timeout=5)

x = np.array([1.5, 2.5, 3.5])
np.array_equal(echo(x), x)     # a float64 vector: True

m = np.arange(6, dtype=np.int32).reshape(2, 3)
np.array_equal(echo(m), m)     # an int32 matrix, dim included: True

echo("hello") == "hello"       # a string: True

d = np.array(["2024-01-01", "2024-01-03"], dtype="datetime64[D]")
np.array_equal(echo(d), d)     # dates keep their meaning: True
```

A data frame crosses as well, with its column types intact.
Here a polars frame with a categorical column; pandas and pyarrow frames work the same way:

```python
import polars as pl
df = pl.DataFrame({
    "total_bill": [16.99, 10.34, 21.01],
    "day": pl.Series(["Sun", "Sun", "Mon"], dtype=pl.Categorical),
})
ch.send(df)        # arrives in R as a data.frame, the categorical column as a factor
back = ch.recv(timeout=5)
back.names         # ('total_bill', 'day')
```

R sees the natural equivalent throughout: a vector for an array, a factor for a category column, a named list for a dict, a `Date` or `POSIXct` for a `datetime64` array.
An Arrow array arrives as an R vector, with Arrow nulls as R missing values: `ch.send(pa.array([1, None, 3]))`.
An ordered categorical — an R ordered factor, a polars `Enum`, an ordered pyarrow dictionary — crosses with its ordering intact.
Labels cross with the values they name: a named R vector arrives as a [`DimArray`](`pymizu.DimArray`) carrying its names, and labels you attach in Python cross to R as `names` or `dimnames`.

## What doesn't cross

Some values have no equivalent on the other side.
pymizu declines them at send time with a `DeclinedError` (a subclass of `TypeError`) that names the offending value on its `path` and `reason` attributes.
The channel stays usable:

```python
import decimal
import pyarrow as pa

tbl = pa.table({"price": pa.array([decimal.Decimal("1.5")])})
try:
    ch.send(tbl)
except pymizu.DeclinedError as e:
    print(e)
    # pymizu: value is not portable to the peer (column 'price': an Arrow type
    # with no portable home (format 'd:2,1'))
ch.close()
```

From Python, also declined: Arrow nested, `date64`, `time`, and `interval` columns.
An Arrow `uint8` column *with nulls* is a `TypeError`: an R raw vector has no `NA`.

From R: a `POSIXlt` time, a character matrix, and S4 objects stay on R's side.
So does a named vector with a class or of character type (a named character vector, factor, `Date`, or `POSIXct`), since names travel only on the plain atomic vectors.
Among data frames: a data.table, a groupedData-style frame (a formula attribute), and a column that is itself a labeled matrix.

The counterpart of the send-time decline is a value that arrives in a language-private format no send gate caught (an attach race, or a misbehaving or version-skewed peer).
The read raises [`ForeignPayloadError`](`pymizu.ForeignPayloadError`) and the message is consumed, so one bad payload never blocks the channel; under `recv_async()`, only that message's waiter rejects.

## pymizu.Frame

A `pymizu.Frame` is Python's home for an R `data.frame`: named columns with a row count.
`frame.to_dict()` returns the columns as a dict: numpy arrays when numpy is installed, memoryviews otherwise, strings and factors as `list[str | None]`.
`frame.names` and `frame.row_names` carry the metadata.

Any Arrow consumer takes a frame in one line: `pl.from_arrow(f)`, `pa.table(f)`, or `pd.DataFrame.from_arrow(f)`.
(With polars >= 2.0, a streaming producer gives a struct Series; `.struct.unnest()` restores the columns.)
Factors become dictionary columns, logicals Arrow `bool`, `Date` `date32`, and `POSIXct` `timestamp[us]`.

A `Frame` pickles, so it crosses Python-to-Python channels.
Sent to R, it becomes a `data.frame` again.

Frame metadata crosses unchanged: a data.frame's full class vector (a tibble's `c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")`, any class ending in `"data.frame"`) and extra attributes travel as-is, stored on the `Frame` uninterpreted.
An unmodified echo restores them in R; a frame rebuilt through pyarrow, polars, pandas, or `from_arrow` arrives in R as a plain `data.frame`.

## Mixed-language pools

A pool's workers can be R processes: `pymizu.r_launcher()` spawns them, and `pymizu.call()` builds a language-neutral task — a qualified `"pkg::fn"` name for R or `"mod.fn"` for Python, or a `source=` string, plus constant arguments:

```python
import numpy as np
import pymizu

pool = pymizu.Pool.create(4, launcher=pymizu.r_launcher())
t = pool.submit(pymizu.call("stats::quantile", np.arange(101.0),
                            probs=np.array([0.25, 0.5, 0.75]), names=False))
print(t.collect())                  # [ 25.  50.  75.]
t2 = pool.submit(pymizu.call(source="y <- x * 2\ny + 1", x=20))
print(t2.collect())                 # 41
pool.stop()
```

Unnamed arguments become positional, keyword arguments named, matching R's calling convention.
A `source=` task runs in a fresh environment with keyword arguments bound as names and positional arguments as `_1`, `_2`, ...; the result is the value of the last expression.

On an R-worker pool, submitting a plain Python callable raises an error naming `pymizu.call()`.
Task errors cross as `TaskError` with the R error type preserved in `remote_type`.
Arguments follow the same rules as channel payloads, zero-copy included: a large array crosses as one shared view, and an array that is already a received view crosses as its name alone.
A pool's workers all run one language — mixing R and Python workers in one pool is not supported.
The reverse direction works the same way: `mizu::mizu_pool()` with `mizu::mizu_py_launcher()`, and `mizu::mizu_submit_call()` with `mizu::mizu_call()` specs.

## Mapping over a foreign pool

To map an R function over Python data, pass a `pymizu.call()` spec as the `fn` of `Pool.map()` or `Pool.map_prepare()` on an R-worker pool.
`mizu::mizu_map()` mirrors this in R:

```python
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
x = np.arange(50.0)
y = 1 + 2 * x + rng.normal(scale=5, size=50)
folds = [
    {"x": xf, "y": yf}
    for xf, yf in zip(x.reshape(5, 10), y.reshape(5, 10))
]

pool = pymizu.Pool.create(4, launcher=pymizu.r_launcher())
pool.map(pymizu.call("stats::median"), list(y.reshape(5, 10))).collect()
pool.map(pymizu.call(source="summary(lm(y ~ x, as.data.frame(x)))$r.squared"),
         folds, template=np.empty(1)).collect()
pool.stop()
```

Each element becomes the spec's first positional argument (or binds as `x` for a `source=` spec).
Put constant arguments in the spec itself; the map's own `args=` and `kwargs=` stay empty.
`template=` and `collect=` work unchanged, and a per-element error crosses with its `index`.
Seeds must be integers in R's 32-bit range.
Each worker language derives its own random streams from the seed, so results are reproducible per worker language but not identical across languages.

## The dtype matrix

The exact correspondence between Python and R dtypes.
Conversion happens once, at send time.
The exact-match rows (float64, int32, int64, complex128, uint8) are a plain memory copy.

| Python sends | R receives | Notes |
|----|----|----|
| `bytes` / uint8 | raw | uint8 with nulls: `TypeError` |
| int8 / int16 / uint16 | integer | widened |
| int32 | integer | |
| uint32 | double | widened |
| int64 | integer64 (bit64's layout) | `INT64_MIN` reads as `NA` |
| uint64 | integer64 (`NA` past 2^63 - 1, warned) | frame column bit-exact |
| float16 / float32 / float64 | double | float16/32 widened |
| bool | logical | |
| complex64 / complex128 | complex | buffer protocol only |
| Arrow bool / numeric with nulls | logical / numeric with `NA` | validity bitmap honored |
| Arrow strings (utf8 / large_utf8 / string_view) | character | Series as a string list |
| Arrow `date32` / `timestamp[u]` | `Date` / `POSIXct` | zone name rides frame metadata |
| Arrow `duration[u]` | `difftime` (secs) | exports back as `duration[us]` |
| timedelta64 (any non-calendar unit) | `difftime` (secs) | `NaT` reads as `NA` |
| Arrow dictionary-encoded | factor | ordered dictionary → ordered factor |
| Arrow ChunkedArray / Table / Series | vector / `data.frame` | chunks concatenated |
| Arrow nested, decimal, time32/64, interval | — | `DeclinedError` |

Missing values cross as sentinels inside the data, and the read rules depend on the accessor.[^missing]

[^missing]: R marks missing values with sentinels inside the data: `INT_MIN` for integer and logical, `INT64_MIN` for integer64, and a special NaN value (`NA_real_`) for double; Arrow nulls convert to these sentinels, so R sees correct `NA`s.
    Read from Python, the result depends on the accessor:

    - Copied reads (`list(...)`, `Frame.to_dict()`) give exact dtypes: a logical arrives as `bool_` when it has no `NA`, else int32.
      An integer arrives as int32 when `NA`-free, else float64 with NaN (every int32 value is exact in float64).
    - Zero-copy views keep the sentinel values in the buffer.
      `.to_numpy()` applies the same rule and checks the region's validity marks for the presence of NAs before scanning any data.
    - int64 keeps its dtype in every numpy form and warns when an `NA` is detected on a copied read or `.to_numpy()`.
      Use `.to_arrow()` for an NA-exact read.
      A genuine Python `-2^63` value round-trips without a warning.
    - Every Arrow export of a logical is Arrow `bool` with a validity bitmap, whatever the path.
      Integer exports are int32 or int64 with a validity bitmap.
      A double exports as float64 with `NA_real_` slots as Arrow nulls (a genuine NaN stays a valid value).

    A genuine int32 value of `-2147483648` collides with the `NA` sentinel and reads as `NA` in R, and an int64 value of `-9223372036854775808` reads as `NA_integer64_`.
    numpy sends stay silent; an Arrow int32 or int64 send with a validity bitmap warns once, to an R peer, while a Python peer reads the identical columns exactly and stays silent.
    Python compute treats `NA_real_` as an ordinary NaN, and whether the exact NaN value survives arithmetic is platform-dependent — do not rely on it.

Round trips are stable after the first hop, and a pass-through echo is bit-exact — even the `NA_real_` value survives a relay through a received view.
A slice or a dtype view of a received view crosses by value.

| Python sends | R sees | Back in Python | Notes |
|----|----|----|----|
| uint8 | raw | uint8 | exact |
| int8 / int16 / uint16 | integer | int32 | widened |
| int32 | integer | int32 | exact |
| uint32 | double | float64 | exact |
| int64 | integer64 | int64 | exact |
| uint64 | integer64 (`NA` past 2^63 - 1, warned) | uint64 | frame column bit-exact |
| float16 | double | float64 | widened |
| float32 | double | float64 | widened |
| float64 | double | float64 | exact |
| bool | logical | `bool_` (int32 with NAs) | dtype lost |
| complex64 / complex128 | complex | complex128 | exact |
| timedelta64 | `difftime` | timedelta64[us] | exact |

| R sends | Python sees | Back in R | Notes |
|----|----|----|----|
| integer | int32 (float64 with NAs) | integer | exact |
| integer64 (bit64) | int64 (warns on `NA`) | integer64 | Python `-2^63` reads as `NA` |
| double | float64 | double | exact |
| raw | uint8 | raw | exact |
| complex | complex128 | complex | exact |
| logical | `bool_` (int32 with NAs) | **integer** | tag lost; whole view stays logical |
| difftime | timedelta64[us] | difftime (secs) | `NA` crosses as `NaT` |

Between two Python processes none of this applies: the exact-match dtypes cross unchanged and everything else pickles.
